O1.brief: Unrealcraft has a few short rules about where to ask for help, where your work is reviewed and what you may post on the Discord server. This first quest checks that you have understood them. You answer five short questions on this page, and you need at least four correct answers.
checklist: Press the Fight button on this page and answer the questions. You need to get at least 4 of the 5 questions right.
O1.done_when: You do not need to send anything for this quest. It is complete as soon as you have passed the quiz on this page.

O2.brief: A specialization is the area of Unreal Engine you want to focus on, such as level design or programming. Your primary specialization decides which quests your path shows you first. You can add more specializations later and you can change your choice at any time, so there is no wrong answer here. In this quest you pick your primary specialization and save it.
checklist: Open your player card page and press Change under Specializations. Pick a primary specialization and press Save. If you have not decided yet, it is fine to choose Undecided.
O2.done_when: You do not need to send anything for this quest. It is complete as soon as a primary specialization is saved on your player card.

O3.brief: The site has three pages that you will come back to often. Your player card shows who you are and how far you have come, the Quest Board lists the quests, and Achievements shows what you have unlocked. On the Quest Board, the part named My path always shows what you should do next. In this quest you open each of these pages once so that you know where they are.
checklist: Open your player card by clicking your name at the top right of the page.
Open the Quest Board and look at the part named My path, which shows the next quests for you.
Go back to your player card page and open Achievements from there.
O3.done_when: You do not need to send anything for this quest. It is complete as soon as you have opened all three pages.

O4.brief: Your player card is the page that other members see when they look at you. You can change how it looks, and more colours, frames and titles become available as you finish quests. In this quest you make a first small change: you write a short motto, which is one line of text about you.
checklist: On your player card page, press Edit profile. Write a short motto and then press Save.
O4.done_when: You do not need to send anything for this quest. It is complete as soon as a motto is saved on your player card.

O5.brief: Most quests end with you sending proof of your work, such as a screenshot or a few lines of text. On the quest page, the place where you send your work is called the chest. In this quest you practice this once with a single word, so that you know how it works before a real quest asks for it.
checklist: Find the chest on this page, type the word READY into it, and press Send.
O5.done_when: Send the word READY through the chest on this page. The quest is complete as soon as this practice work is sent.

PQ17.brief: C++ is the programming language that Unreal Engine itself is written in. Programmers use it to build features and then make some of them visible to the editor and to Blueprints. A header file, which ends in .h, lists what a C++ class contains, and special words such as UCLASS, UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION mark what the engine and the editor can see. In this quest you do not write any code: you read one header file and learn what these words mean.
checklist: Read the Programming Quick Start page in the Unreal Engine documentation. You do not need an IDE, which is a program for writing code, to follow along.

Open the example Actor .h file from the quick start. You can read it in the documentation, or open any header in the Source folder of a C++ template project. In it, find UCLASS(), GENERATED_BODY(), one UPROPERTY and one UFUNCTION.
Look at the words inside the UPROPERTY brackets, which are called specifiers: EditAnywhere, VisibleAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite and Category. Match each one to what it does.
Work out where that UPROPERTY would appear in the Details panel when the actor is placed in a level. Look for the heading that has the same name as its Category.
Bonus, optional: install the IDE, compile the quick start actor, and place it in a level.
PQ17.done_when: Send 3 lines that say what UCLASS, UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION each do, and a screenshot of a C++ property in the Details panel. Compiling is optional, but say whether you did it.

PQ18.brief: The Gameplay Ability System, often shortened to GAS, is a framework inside Unreal for things characters can do, such as attacks, heals and dashes, and for the numbers these actions change, such as health. Many Unreal games use it, so you will hear its words often. In this quest you do not build anything: you read the overview and learn the five main terms well enough to describe a game mechanic with them.
checklist: Read the Gameplay Ability System overview page in the Unreal Engine documentation. You can skip the code samples if you like.
Write a one-line definition for each of these five terms: Ability System Component, Gameplay Ability, Attribute, Gameplay Effect, and Gameplay Tag.
Pick a mechanic from a game you know, such as a dash, a heal or a stun. Describe how it works using those five terms.
Name one thing in your own levels that could apply a Gameplay Effect, for example a hazard, a pickup or a zone.
PQ18.done_when: Send your five one-line definitions and your description of the mechanic. You also need to pass the quiz of this quest.

EAQ22.brief: Players look first at the brightest part of the screen and at the places with the most contrast. This means lighting is a tool for guiding the player, not only for making a level look good. In this quest you do one lighting pass on the level that has your pickup game, so that the pickups and the way to them are easy to see.
checklist: Open the level that contains the pickup and win loop you built earlier. Move the camera to the view the player has at the start, and save a camera bookmark there (Ctrl plus a number key).
Set up the basic lighting with the Env. Light Mixer window. Use it to add a Directional Light, a Sky Light, a Sky Atmosphere and Height Fog.
Make each pickup stand out. You can put a small Point Light on it, or you can place the pickup in the brightest area.
Make the dead ends darker or less noticeable, so that the player sees the route to the pickups first.

Add a Post Process Volume and turn on Infinite Extent so that it affects the whole level. Then bring the minimum and maximum values of the auto exposure closer together, so that the brightness does not jump when the player moves between rooms.
EAQ22.done_when: Send one screenshot from before and one from after your lighting pass, both taken from the same camera bookmark. Add one line that says how a player finds the first pickup now.

GDQ5.brief: A win condition is the rule that says when the player has won. Together with something to collect, it makes the smallest complete game you can build. The count of collected coins is kept in the GameMode, a Blueprint that holds the rules of the game and stays alive while the coins are destroyed. In this quest you make coins the player can pick up, count them, and show a win message when all three are collected.
checklist: Create a Blueprint named BP_UUGameMode as a child of the GameMode of your template. Give it an Integer variable named Collected, and an Integer variable named Target that is Instance Editable and set to 3. Then set BP_UUGameMode as the GameMode Override of the level.

Make a Blueprint named BP_Coin with a mesh and a sphere trigger that only reacts to the player (as you did in SQ9). On overlap, use Get Game Mode, then Cast to BP_UUGameMode, then call a function named AddCoin, and after that call Destroy Actor.
Inside the AddCoin function, add 1 to Collected. Then use a Branch node that checks whether Collected >= Target.
On the True output of the Branch, show a win message. A Print String node is enough, and a widget on screen is a bonus.
Place 3 coins in the level in spots where the player has to move around to reach them. Play in the editor (PIE) until you win.
GDQ5.done_when: Send a clip of less than 30 seconds, recorded while playing in the editor, that shows you collecting all 3 coins and the win message appearing. Also send a screenshot of the AddCoin function.

EAQ23.brief: A master material is one material built with parameters, which are values such as a color or a roughness that you leave open to change. From it you make Material Instances, which are light copies that only change those parameters. This way one material can give many objects different looks. In this quest you build a small master material and three instances, and use their colors to show the player what each object in your level is for.
checklist: Create a new material named M_UC_Master in the folder /Content/UC/Materials.

Add these parameters to it: a Vector parameter named BaseColor, two Scalar parameters named Roughness and Metallic, and a Scalar parameter named EmissiveStrength. Multiply EmissiveStrength by the color and connect the result to the Emissive input.
Give every parameter a Group in its Details panel. Groups keep the parameter list tidy when you open an instance.
Make 3 Material Instances from it: MI_Gameplay_Interact (bright, with a little emissive glow), MI_Gameplay_Hazard (red), and MI_Gameplay_Neutral (matte gray).
Apply the instances to the interactable objects you built in your earlier quests, so that players can tell the role of each object by its color.
EAQ23.done_when: Send a screenshot of the master material graph, and a screenshot of the 3 instances applied in your level.
